u1.text: "It is very good, sir. When a person has nothing to eat, fasting is the smartest thing he could do. When, for example, Siddhartha hadn't learned to fast, he would have to accept any kind of service before that day is up, whether it may be with you or wherever, because hunger would force him to do so. But like this, Siddhartha can wait calmly, he knows no impatience, he knows no emergency, for a long time he can allow hunger to besiege him and can laugh about it. This, sir, is what fasting is good for."

u2.text: Twice a day, a plentiful meal was served, but Siddhartha only ate once a day, and ate neither meat nor did he drink wine. Kamaswami told him about his trade, showed him the merchandise and storage rooms, showed him calculations. Siddhartha got to know many new things, he heard a lot and spoke little. And thinking of Kamala's words, he was never subservient to the merchant, forced him to treat him as an equal, yes even more than an equal. Kamaswami conducted his business with care and often with passion, but Siddhartha looked upon all of this as if it was a game, the rules of which he tried hard to learn precisely, but the contents of which did not touch his heart.

u3.text: He soon saw that Siddhartha knew little about rice and wool, shipping and trade, but that he acted in a fortunate manner, and that Siddhartha surpassed him, the merchant, in calmness and equanimity, and in the art of listening and deeply understanding previously unknown people. "This Brahmin," he said to a friend, "is no proper merchant and will never be one, there is never any passion in his soul when he conducts our business. But he has that mysterious quality of those people to whom success comes all by itself, whether this may be a good star of his birth, magic, or something he has learned among Samanas. He always seems to be merely playing with our business affairs, they never fully become a part of him, they never rule over him, he is never afraid of failure, he is never upset by a loss."

u4.text: At one time, he travelled to a village to buy a large harvest of rice there. But when he got there, the rice had already been sold to another merchant. Nevertheless, Siddhartha stayed for several days in that village, treated the farmers for a drink, gave copper-coins to their children, joined in the celebration of a wedding, and returned extremely satisfied from his trip. Kamaswami held against him that he had not turned back right away, that he had wasted time and money. Siddhartha answered: "Stop scolding, dear friend! Nothing was ever achieved by scolding. If a loss has occurred, let me bear that loss. I am very satisfied with this trip. I have gotten to know many kinds of people, a Brahmin has become my friend, children have sat on my knees, farmers have shown me their fields, nobody knew that I was a merchant."

u5.text: Look, my dear, if I had been Kamaswami, I would have travelled back, being annoyed and in a hurry, as soon as I had seen that my purchase had been rendered impossible, and time and money would indeed have been lost. But like this, I've had a few good days, I've learned, had joy, I've neither harmed myself nor others by annoyance and hastiness. And if I'll ever return there again, perhaps to buy an upcoming harvest, or for whatever purpose it might be, friendly people will receive me in a friendly and happy manner, and I will praise myself for not showing any hurry and displeasure at that time.

u6.text: Indeed his soul was not with the trade. The business was good enough to provide him with the money for Kamala, and it earned him much more than he needed. Besides from this, Siddhartha's interest and curiosity was only concerned with the people, whose businesses, crafts, worries, pleasures, and acts of foolishness used to be as alien and distant to him as the moon.

u7.text: He saw mankind going through life in a childlike or animallike manner, which he loved and also despised at the same time. He saw them toiling, saw them suffering, and becoming gray for the sake of things which seemed to him to entirely unworthy of this price, for money, for little pleasures, for being slightly honoured, he saw them scolding and insulting each other, he saw them complaining about pain at which a Samana would only smile, and suffering because of deprivations which a Samana would not feel.

u8.text: At times he felt, deep in his chest, a dying, quiet voice, which admonished him quietly, lamented quietly; he hardly perceived it. And then, for an hour, he became aware of the strange life he was leading, of him doing lots of things which were only a game, of, though being happy and feeling joy at times, real life still passing him by and not touching him. As a ballplayer plays with his balls, he played with his business deals, with the people around him, watched them, found amusement in them; with his heart, with the source of his being, he was not with them. The source ran somewhere, far away from him, ran and ran invisibly, had nothing to do with his life any more.

u9.text: "No," said Siddhartha, "that's not the reason why. Kamaswami is just as smart as I, and still has no refuge in himself. Others have it, who are small children with respect to their mind. Most people, Kamala, are like a falling leaf, which is blown and is turning around through the air, and wavers, and tumbles to the ground. But others, a few, are like stars, they go on a fixed course, no wind reaches them, in themselves they have their law and their course.

u10.text: When, one day, Kamaswami held against him that he had learned everything he knew from him, he replied: "Would you please not kid me with such jokes! What I've learned from you is how much a basket of fish costs and how much interests may be charged on loaned money. These are your areas of expertise. I haven't learned to think from you, my dear Kamaswami, you ought to be the one seeking to learn from me."

u11.text: "You are the best lover," she said thoughtfully, "I ever saw. You're stronger than others, more supple, more willing. You've learned my art well, Siddhartha. At some time, when I'll be older, I'd want to bear your child. And yet, my dear, you've remained a Samana, and yet you do not love me, you love nobody. Isn't it so?" "It might very well be so," Siddhartha said tiredly. "I am like you. You also do not love—how else could you practise love as a craft? Perhaps people of our kind can't love. The childlike people can; that's their secret."

A.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?
options: Fasting makes him weak, so he must take any work the merchant offers.
Siddhartha fasts mainly to please and impress Kamala.
Fasting lets Siddhartha wait calmly instead of being forced by hunger.
Siddhartha thinks fasting is useless for life in the city.
A.explanation: He explains that without fasting, "hunger would force him" to take any service, but "like this, Siddhartha can wait calmly." The choice saying fasting makes him weak reverses this. He calls fasting "very good," not useless. Kamala is not mentioned in his explanation. The point of the passage is that fasting frees him from need, not that it weakens him.

A.prompt: According to the passage, how often did Siddhartha eat while living in the merchant's house?
options: Never in the house
Only when Kamaswami ate
Once a day
Twice a day, with meat and wine
A.explanation: Although "twice a day, a plentiful meal was served," "Siddhartha only ate once a day" and took neither meat nor wine. So "twice a day" describes what was served, not what he ate. Nothing ties his meals to Kamaswami's. He did eat there, once daily.

A.prompt: As used in the passage, "expertise" most nearly means
options: a loan
a trading journey
a joke
special knowledge
A.explanation: "These are your areas of expertise" follows the price of fish and interest on loans, so it means special knowledge. A trading journey is not the sense. "A loan" is one topic, not the meaning. "Joke" echoes "such jokes" earlier but does not fit "areas of."

A.prompt: Siddhartha's behaviour in the village suggests that he
options: plans to buy the whole village for himself
is angry that another merchant bought the rice first
dislikes children and the noise they make
values people and experiences more than profit
A.explanation: Though the rice was sold, he stayed, joined a wedding, gave coins to children, and "returned extremely satisfied," valuing people over profit. He shows no anger. Buying the village is never suggested. "Children have sat on my knees," so he does not dislike them.

A.prompt: Based on the passage, what does Kamaswami say is missing when Siddhartha conducts business?
options: Patience
Passion
Knowledge of reading
Success in trade
A.explanation: Kamaswami says "there is never any passion in his soul when he conducts our business." He says success "comes all by itself," so success is not missing. Siddhartha surpasses him in calmness, so patience is present. He reads well, as earlier shown.

A.prompt: Which choice provides the best evidence for the answer to the previous question?
options: "But he has that mysterious quality of those people to whom success comes all by itself"
"Siddhartha surpassed him, the merchant, in calmness and equanimity"
"he is never afraid of failure"
"there is never any passion in his soul when he conducts our business"
A.explanation: Only "never any passion in his soul" names what is missing. The "success comes all by itself" line names what he has. "Never afraid of failure" shows calm, not a lack of passion directly. "Surpassed him... in calmness" is the narrator's comparison, not Kamaswami's statement of what is missing.

A.prompt: The list "for money, for little pleasures, for being slightly honoured" mainly serves to
options: list the goals a Samana strives for
explain how Kamaswami became so rich
show how small the things people suffer for seem to Siddhartha
name the gifts Siddhartha brings Kamala each day in her garden
A.explanation: He sees people "becoming gray for the sake of things which seemed to him... entirely unworthy," then lists money and little pleasures, showing how small they seem. These are not gifts to Kamala. Kamaswami is not discussed. A Samana would "only smile" at these.

A.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?
options: Siddhartha senses that real life is passing him by.
Siddhartha decides to leave the city at once.
Siddhartha becomes a skilled and famous ballplayer.
Siddhartha feels fully alive and throws his heart into his business.
A.explanation: He becomes aware of "real life still passing him by and not touching him." The choice saying he feels fully alive reverses his detachment; "with his heart... he was not with them." He wishes for change but does not leave here. The ballplayer is a comparison, not a new skill.

A.prompt: According to the passage, what had happened when Siddhartha reached the village?
options: The rice had already been sold to another merchant.
Kamaswami was already waiting for him there.
The harvest had failed after the long rains.
The farmers would sell only at twice the price.
A.explanation: The passage says "when he got there, the rice had already been sold to another merchant." No higher price is demanded. The harvest did not fail; it was sold. Kamaswami was not there; he scolds Siddhartha after his return. The lost purchase is what prompts Kamaswami's later complaint about the wasted journey.

A.prompt: As used in the passage, "despised" most nearly means
options: feared
held in contempt
ignored
loved and admired
A.explanation: He "loved and also despised" mankind "at the same time," so despised is set against loved and means held in contempt. "Loved and admired" gives only the "loved" half. He does not fear them. He watches them closely, so he does not ignore them.

A.prompt: Kamala's words suggest that she suspects Siddhartha
options: cannot truly love anyone
is still a skilled Samana at heart
wants to become a merchant
loves her more than any man ever has
A.explanation: She says "you do not love me, you love nobody. Isn't it so?" and he agrees it "might very well be so." She calls him "the best lover" in skill, not in deep love. He has left the forest. Becoming a merchant is not her concern here.

A.prompt: The comparison of most people to "a falling leaf" suggests that they
options: are about to die soon
are pushed about by outside forces
grow strong over time
follow a fixed course untouched by wind
A.explanation: A leaf "is blown and is turning around through the air," so most people are pushed by outside forces. The stars, not the leaves, follow "a fixed course." The image is about direction, not death. Falling and tumbling do not suggest growing strong.

B.prompt: According to the passage, in what did Siddhartha surpass the merchant?
options: Knowledge of rice, wool and shipping
Speed at counting coins
Love of money and gain
Calmness and the art of listening
B.explanation: Siddhartha "surpassed him... in calmness and equanimity, and in the art of listening." The passage says he "knew little about rice and wool, shipping and trade." Love of money is what he lacks. Counting speed is not mentioned. The passage sets his inner calm against the merchant's knowledge of goods and trade.

B.prompt: As used in the passage, "equanimity" most nearly means
options: composure
stubbornness
wealth
equal shares
B.explanation: Paired with "calmness" and with never being "upset by a loss," equanimity means composure. "Equal shares" plays on "equal" but is the friend's later advice, not this word. "Wealth" and "stubbornness" do not fit the calm the passage praises. His composure shows when he loses money and still remains calm and unworried.

B.prompt: The passage suggests that, for Siddhartha, the merchant's business is
options: a skill he had already known as a boy
the most important purpose of his whole life, more important than Kamala
a game whose rules interest him but whose content does not move him
a heavy burden he hates
B.explanation: He looked upon it "as if it was a game, the rules of which he tried hard to learn," but "the contents of which did not touch his heart." It is not his life's purpose. He does not hate it. He "got to know many new things," so it was new to him.

B.prompt: What does Siddhartha say he learned from Kamaswami?
options: Nothing at all of any use
How to fast and wait patiently
Only practical facts such as prices and interest
How to think clearly about every problem he meets
B.explanation: He says he learned "how much a basket of fish costs and how much interests may be charged." He says "I haven't learned to think from you," so thinking clearly is wrong. Fasting and waiting are his Samana skills. He admits learning prices, so not nothing.

B.prompt: Which choice provides the best evidence for the answer to the previous question?
options: "I haven't learned to think from you, my dear Kamaswami"
"how much a basket of fish costs and how much interests may be charged on loaned money"
"Would you please not kid me with such jokes!"
"When, one day, Kamaswami held against him that he had learned everything he knew from him"
B.explanation: Only the line about the basket of fish and interest names what he learned. The opening line is Kamaswami's claim. "Would you please not kid me" rejects the claim without naming anything. "I haven't learned to think from you" says what he did not learn.

B.prompt: Siddhartha's statement beginning "if I had been Kamaswami" mainly serves to
options: contrast how each man would react to the lost purchase
explain the price of rice in the village
show that Siddhartha wishes to become the merchant himself
praise Kamaswami's quick decisions in trade
B.explanation: He imagines Kamaswami returning "annoyed and in a hurry," then contrasts his own "few good days," so it contrasts reactions. He does not wish to be Kamaswami. The hurry is criticized, not praised. Rice prices are not discussed. The contrast lets Siddhartha defend his calm, friendly way against the merchant's hurry.

B.prompt: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?
options: Siddhartha works hard at trade because he needs the money.
Siddhartha's real interest lies in people, not in trade.
Siddhartha dislikes nearly all the people of the city.
Siddhartha studies the moon and the stars.
B.explanation: "His soul was not with the trade," and his real interest lay with the people. The business "earned him much more than he needed," so he does not need every coin. He is curious about people, not hostile. The moon is a comparison only.

B.prompt: As used in the passage, "lamented" most nearly means
options: sang happily
commanded
laughed loudly
mourned
B.explanation: The voice "admonished him quietly, lamented quietly," so it mourned. Laughing is the opposite of the grieving voice. "Commanded" overstates a quiet, dying voice. "Sang happily" contradicts the sadness of a "dying, quiet voice." The voice is the remnant of his inner life, quietly grieving over what he is losing.

B.prompt: The contrast between the falling leaf and the stars mainly serves to
options: describe the night sky over the city on the evening of their talk
divide people into those without and those with an inner law
praise the followers of Gotama above all others
show that Kamala herself is like a falling leaf
B.explanation: Leaves are "blown," while stars "have their law and their course" in themselves, dividing people by inner law. It is a comparison, not weather. He says Kamala is like him, not a leaf. Gotama's followers are not mentioned in this passage, so it cannot be praising them.

B.prompt: Siddhartha's explanation suggests that fasting gives him
options: freedom from having to accept any offer out of need
a reason to refuse every job a merchant offers
a clever way to make more money
great hunger and weakness in the body
B.explanation: Because hunger cannot "force him," he can wait and choose, so fasting frees him from need-driven choices. He is not refusing every job; he is talking with Kamaswami. He says he can "laugh about" hunger, not that it weakens him. Fasting does not earn money directly.

B.prompt: The passage presents Siddhartha mainly through
options: Govinda's letters to him
Kamala's memories of him
Siddhartha's own account of his years in trade
Kamaswami's view of him as an unusual partner
B.explanation: After the narrator's summary, Kamaswami tells "a friend" what he thinks of "This Brahmin," so we see Siddhartha through Kamaswami's eyes. Siddhartha does not speak. Kamala and Govinda do not appear, and no letters are mentioned. The narrator lets Kamaswami describe how strange and calm his partner seems in business.

B.prompt: How does Passage 2 add to the interest described in Passage 1?
options: It shows him returning eagerly to his trade.
It shows that he now shares all the worries, hopes and joys of the city people around him.
It shows that his interest in people is mixed with a sense of distance and scorn.
It shows him losing all interest in people.
B.explanation: Passage 1 shows his curiosity about people; Passage 2 says he "loved and also despised" them and saw them as childlike. He is not like them; he smiles at their pains as a Samana. His interest continues. Trade is not the focus of Passage 2.

C.prompt: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?
options: Only a few people have a steady law within themselves.
Kamaswami is wiser than Siddhartha in everything.
Smart people always have a refuge within, while others never do.
All of Gotama's followers have found peace.
C.explanation: Most are "like a falling leaf," but "a few, are like stars" with "their law" in themselves. Siddhartha denies smartness is the reason ("Kamaswami is just as smart"). No one is said here to have found peace. He calls Kamaswami "just as smart" but without refuge, not wiser.

C.prompt: The passage suggests that Siddhartha's life in the city
options: is full of danger
fully satisfies him and leaves nothing to wish for
is exactly like a Samana's life
lacks the deep involvement of his heart
C.explanation: "With his heart, with the source of his being, he was not with them," so his life lacks heart. He longs to truly live, so he is not fully satisfied. No danger is described. He plays with business and pleasure, unlike a Samana.

C.prompt: Siddhartha's list "a Brahmin has become my friend, children have sat on my knees, farmers have shown me their fields" mainly serves to
options: describe the village wedding he attended
show what he valued in the trip despite the lost purchase
prove that the rice will be sold to him cheaply next year
show that he was lonely on the journey
C.explanation: Answering Kamaswami's scolding, he lists friendships and kindness to show what he gained. No promise about next year's rice is made here. The wedding is mentioned earlier, not in this list. The list shows companionship, not loneliness. Each item in the list names a human connection, not a profit, which is his point.

C.prompt: Why does Siddhartha think his way of handling the lost purchase was better?
options: It pleased Kamala and made her laugh.
It taught him how to scold others.
It gave him good days and future goodwill instead of wasted anger.
It let him buy the next harvest more cheaply than other merchants.
C.explanation: He had "a few good days" and expects "friendly people will receive me" next time, avoiding "annoyance and hastiness." No price deal is mentioned. Kamala is not involved. He tells Kamaswami not to scold, so he learned no scolding. He judges the trip by the friendships it made rather than by money lost.

C.prompt: Which choice provides the best evidence for the answer to the previous question?
options: "I would have travelled back, being annoyed and in a hurry"
"or for whatever purpose it might be"
"Look, my dear, if I had been Kamaswami"
"friendly people will receive me in a friendly and happy manner"
C.explanation: Only "friendly people will receive me" names the future goodwill his calm earned. The "annoyed and in a hurry" line describes the alternative he rejects. "If I had been Kamaswami" introduces the contrast. "Whatever purpose it might be" is a passing phrase without the benefit.

C.prompt: As used in the passage, "toiling" most nearly means
options: resting at ease
travelling
labouring hard
praying
C.explanation: He saw people "toiling... suffering, and becoming gray," so toiling means hard labour. Resting and pleasure reverse the sense. "Travelling" and "praying" are other activities, but the word is paired with suffering and growing gray from effort. The word belongs to his outside view of people labouring and suffering for small rewards.

C.prompt: The comparison "As a ballplayer plays with his balls" suggests that Siddhartha handles his affairs
options: clumsily, dropping and losing many deals
skilfully but without real involvement
angrily
with deep passion
C.explanation: A ballplayer plays skilfully, and Siddhartha "played with his business deals... with his heart... he was not with them." Nothing suggests clumsiness; he succeeds. He is amused, not angry. The passage says he lacks passion, wishing he could act with passion.

C.prompt: Siddhartha's reply suggests that he sees himself and Kamala as
options: fellow Samanas who still live by forest rules
completely different, since she loves deeply and he does not love at all
alike in being unable to love as the childlike people do
innocent children who know nothing of the world
C.explanation: He says "I am like you. You also do not love," and "The childlike people can; that's their secret," so they are alike and unlike the childlike. "Completely different" denies their likeness. He contrasts them with the childlike. Only he has been a Samana.

C.prompt: The final sentence "you ought to be the one seeking to learn from me" mainly serves to
options: apologize for all the money lost on the journey
reverse Kamaswami's claim about who taught whom
ask Kamaswami for a loan
end their partnership
C.explanation: Kamaswami claimed Siddhartha learned everything from him; Siddhartha turns this around. He does not apologize. No loan is asked. He does not end the partnership here; he only answers the claim. The ending turns the merchant's boast into a gentle claim that Siddhartha is the real teacher between them.

C.prompt: The narrator's description of mankind in the passage mainly reflects
options: the view of the gods
the merchants' own pride in their hard work
Kamala's opinion of her visitors
Siddhartha's detached view from the outside
C.explanation: People are seen as "childlike or animallike," suffering pains "at which a Samana would only smile," so the view is Siddhartha's detached one. The merchants' pride is not given. Kamala and the gods are not the viewpoint here. The narration adopts his outside, half-amused view of the people around him.

C.prompt: What do the two passages together suggest about Siddhartha?
options: He values his Samana skills above the merchant's knowledge.
He has never learned anything of value.
He now depends entirely on Kamaswami's teaching for success.
He wants to become Kamaswami's servant.
C.explanation: Passage 1 praises fasting; Passage 2 says he learned only prices from Kamaswami, who "ought to be the one seeking to learn" from him. He has not given up his skills. He refuses to be a servant. He clearly learned both kinds of things.

C.prompt: What do both passages suggest is missing from Siddhartha's life?
options: Wholehearted involvement and love
Friends
Skill in love
Money and success in trade
C.explanation: In Passage 1 his heart "was not with them"; in Passage 2 Kamala says "you love nobody." His business succeeds and Kamala is with him. She praises his skill. He has many companions, but both passages point to a missing heart.
